Title: ETDI: Mitigating Tool Squatting and Rug Pull Attacks in Model Context Protocol (MCP) by Using OAuth-Enhanced Tool Definitions and Policy-Based Access Control
Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) plays a crucial role in extending the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by enabling integration with external tools and data sources. However, the standard MCP specification presents significant security vulnerabilities, notably Tool Poisoning and Rug Pull attacks. This paper introduces the Enhanced Tool Definition Interface (ETDI), a security extension designed to fortify MCP. ETDI incorporates cryptographic identity verification, immutable versioned tool definitions, and explicit permission management, often leveraging OAuth 2.0. We further propose extending MCP with fine-grained, policy-based access control, where tool capabilities are dynamically evaluated against explicit policies using a dedicated policy engine, considering runtime context beyond static OAuth scopes. This layered approach aims to establish a more secure, trustworthy, and controllable ecosystem for AI applications interacting with LLMs and external tools.
Major_Contribution_Result: ETDI proposes hardening Model Context Protocol tool use via cryptographically verified identities, immutable versioned tool definitions, OAuth-enhanced permission/scope management, and an optional fine-grained policy-engine layer (e.g., Cedar/OPA) for runtime contextual authorization. The paper argues this layered design mitigates MCP tool poisoning/squatting and rug-pull style definition changes; security analysis is primarily design-level rather than large-scale empirical ASR reporting.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: In the Discussion, the authors list adoption challenges for ETDI and its extensions: implementation complexity for tool providers and MCP client/server developers; performance overhead from JWT validation and remote policy checks; secure key and policy lifecycle management; UX difficulty of re-approval and explaining complex policies; need for broad ecosystem adoption/standardization; and certification that MCP components faithfully enforce policy checks without bypass.
Critics: This is a protocol/architecture mitigation proposal for MCP tool trust, with discussion of adoption challenges (complexity, latency, key/policy management, UX, ecosystem certification) but without a dedicated empirical agent-benchmark evaluation in the recovered text. For LLM-agent security SLRs it covers supply-chain/tool-definition integrity more than prompt-injection ASR. Do not treat it as experimentally ranking against AgentShield or similar systems.
